teaching.causalExplanation: A stem-and-leaf plot keeps every value. The stem is the leading digit, the leaf is the last digit, and the key tells you how they join. Two, four is twenty-four runs. Without the key, two four could just as easily mean two point four. The leaves are in order, so the batter's fifteen scores run from nought, four and seven, up to eighty-seven. How many times did the batter score thirty or more? Count the leaves from the three stem down. Thirty-three, thirty-six, forty-one, fifty-eight, sixty-three, eighty-seven. Six innings. And because the values are in order, the middle score is easy to find. Fifteen scores, so the eighth one, twenty-four. In context, this batter usually scores under forty, with the occasional big innings. To compare two batters, share the stems. Batter B's leaves go to the right, as usual. Batter A's leaves go to the left, reading outwards from the stem, so four, two on the left is twenty-four, not forty-two. Now compare row by row. Batter A has three scores under ten, and Batter B has just one. Batter A also has the three biggest scores, fifty-eight, sixty-three and eighty-seven, while Batter B never passes forty-five. Their middle scores are close, twenty-four and twenty-eight. So Batter B is the more consistent batter, and Batter A is more likely to fail, or to win you the game. The same season, from the bowler's end. This dot plot shows how many wickets one bowler took in each of sixteen matches. Each dot is one match, sitting above its number of wickets. Every dot is a real match, so nothing is grouped or lost. The tallest stack is above two, so two wickets was the most common result. In how many matches did she take three or more wickets? Count the dots, not the heights. Three above three, one above four, one above five, five matches. A dot plot shows every value and where they bunch up, and it works best for small sets of numbers, like these.

Batter A's leaves go to the left, reading outwards from the stem, so four, two on the left is twenty-four, not forty-two. Now compare row by row. scenes.teachingReason: A line graph shows change over time. Here's a phone's battery level through one day, measured ten times through the day, from a hundred per cent at seven in the morning. scenes.teachingReason: Sector graphs and divided bar charts both show parts of one whole. Here's a student's two hundred dollar weekly budget as a sector graph. The whole circle is three hundred and sixty degrees, so each sector's share is its angle out of three sixty. Food is a hundred and eight degrees. That's a hundred and eight out of three sixty, thirty per cent, and thirty per cent of two hundred dollars is sixty dollars. Now unroll the circle into a bar. Same parts, same order, now as lengths. A divided bar chart works the same way, with length instead of angle. Either way, the parts must add to the whole, a full circle or the full bar. This twenty centimetre bar shows how our two hundred Year 11 students get to school. Bus takes six centimetres, six out of twenty, thirty per cent, sixty students. The angle or the length gives the share. The share times the total gives the amount.
